title: Ethiopian English University Entrance Practice Test 16 2024
description: Ethiopian English University Entrance Practice Test 16 2024 featuring 100 authentic questions with step-by-step solutions. Designed for Ethiopian national exam mastery.

questions.questionText: The committee approved the proposal after several hours of discussion.
options: The committee approved the proposal, after several hours of discussion.
The committee approved the proposal after several hours of discussion.
The committee approved, the proposal after several hours of discussion.
The committee approved the proposal; after several hours of discussion.
questions.explanation: The introductory phrase is not separated from the main clause here, so no comma is required.

questions.questionText: Which sentence is correctly punctuated?
options: Although the weather was terrible we continued the journey.
Although the weather was terrible; we continued the journey.
Although the weather was terrible, we continued the journey.
Although, the weather was terrible we continued the journey.
questions.explanation: A comma separates the introductory dependent clause from the independent clause.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses a semicolon?
options: The examination was difficult; however, most students remained calm.
The examination was difficult, however; most students remained calm.
The examination was difficult; however most students, remained calm.
The examination was difficult however; most students remained calm.
questions.explanation: A semicolon can join independent clauses, while however is followed by a comma.

questions.questionText: Which sentence contains a correctly punctuated direct question?
options: She asked me where I lived?
She asked me, where did I live?
She asked me where I lived.
She asked me where I lived!
questions.explanation: An indirect question ends with a period, not a question mark.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly punctuates the direct quotation?
options: The teacher said "You must revise this chapter."
The teacher said, "You must revise this chapter."
The teacher said; "You must revise this chapter."
The teacher said: "You must revise this chapter."
questions.explanation: A comma commonly separates a reporting clause from a following direct quotation.

questions.questionText: Which sentence uses the apostrophe correctly?
options: The childrens' books were on the teachers desk.
The children's books were on the teacher's desk.
The childrens books were on the teacher's desk.
The children's books were on the teachers desk.
questions.explanation: Children is an irregular plural, so possession takes 's; teacher's is singular possessive.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly distinguishes its from it's?
options: The company changed it's policy because its ineffective.
The company changed its policy because it's ineffective.
The company changed it's policy because it's ineffective.
The company changed its' policy because its ineffective.
questions.explanation: Its shows possession; it's means it is.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses a colon?
options: She brought: three books, a notebook, and a calculator.
She brought three things: three books, a notebook, and a calculator.
She brought three things, three books: a notebook, and a calculator.
She brought three things; three books, a notebook, and a calculator.
questions.explanation: The complete clause before the colon appropriately introduces the list.

questions.questionText: Which sentence contains a comma splice?
options: The road was flooded, so the buses stopped.
The road was flooded; the buses stopped.
The road was flooded, the buses stopped.
The road was flooded. The buses stopped.
questions.explanation: Two independent clauses are joined only by a comma.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses a dash for emphasis?
options: She had one choice—leave immediately.
She had one choice, leave immediately.
She had one choice; leave immediately.
She had one choice:—leave immediately.
questions.explanation: A dash can create a strong break before an emphasized conclusion.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses parentheses?
options: The conference (which begins tomorrow will last three days.
The conference, (which begins tomorrow), will last three days.
The conference (which begins tomorrow) will last three days.
The conference which (begins tomorrow) will last three days.
questions.explanation: Parentheses enclose removable additional information.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses an apostrophe in a regular plural possessive?
options: The students's books were collected.
The student's books were collected.
The students' books were collected.
The students books' were collected.
questions.explanation: A regular plural ending in s takes an apostrophe after the s.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses a hyphen?
options: She is a well known researcher.
She is a well-known researcher.
She is a well—known researcher.
She is a well;known researcher.
questions.explanation: Well-known is a compound adjective before a noun and is hyphenated.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses a hyphen in an age expression before a noun?
options: They hired a twenty five year old assistant.
They hired a twenty-five-year-old assistant.
They hired a twenty-five year-old assistant.
They hired a twenty five-year-old assistant.
questions.explanation: All parts of the compound adjective are hyphenated before the noun.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses commas for direct address?
options: Please, Dawit submit the report.
Please Dawit, submit the report.
Please, Dawit, submit the report.
Please Dawit submit, the report.
questions.explanation: The person's name is a direct address and is set off with commas.

questions.questionText: Which sentence has the punctuation needed to make the intended meaning clear?
options: Let's eat Grandma!
Let's eat, Grandma!
Let's eat; Grandma!
Let's eat: Grandma!
questions.explanation: The comma shows that Grandma is being addressed rather than identified as food.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly punctuates a list containing internal commas?
options: We visited Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, Nairobi, Kenya, and Kampala, Uganda.
We visited Addis Ababa, Ethiopia; Nairobi, Kenya; and Kampala, Uganda.
We visited Addis Ababa; Ethiopia, Nairobi; Kenya, and Kampala; Uganda.
We visited Addis Ababa: Ethiopia; Nairobi: Kenya; and Kampala: Uganda.
questions.explanation: Semicolons clearly separate the major list items that already contain commas.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses a comma before a coordinating conjunction?
options: She studied hard and she passed the examination.
She studied hard, and she passed the examination.
She studied hard; and she passed the examination.
She studied hard: and she passed the examination.
questions.explanation: A comma is used before and when it joins two independent clauses.

questions.questionText: Which sentence does NOT require a comma before and?
options: He opened the door, and he entered the room.
She bought a pen, and she gave it to me.
They bought bread and milk.
I wanted to leave, but the rain continued.
questions.explanation: Bread and milk are simple items in a compound object, not independent clauses.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly punctuates an introductory phrase?
options: After the examination the students left quietly.
After the examination, the students left quietly.
After, the examination the students left quietly.
After the examination; the students left quietly.
questions.explanation: The introductory phrase is followed by a comma.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly punctuates a non-essential relative clause?
options: My brother who lives in Addis Ababa is a doctor.
My brother, who lives in Addis Ababa, is a doctor.
My brother who lives in Addis Ababa, is a doctor.
My brother, who lives in Addis Ababa is a doctor.
questions.explanation: The non-essential information is enclosed by commas.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly avoids commas around essential information?
options: Students, who study regularly, usually perform well.
Students who study regularly usually perform well.
Students, who study regularly usually perform well.
Students who study regularly, usually perform well.
questions.explanation: The relative clause identifies the students being discussed and is therefore essential.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses an exclamation mark?
options: What an incredible performance!
What an incredible performance?
What an incredible performance.
What an incredible performance;
questions.explanation: The sentence expresses strong emotion, so an exclamation mark is appropriate.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses a question mark?
options: Why did you leave the meeting.
Why did you leave the meeting!
Why did you leave the meeting?
Why did you leave the meeting;
questions.explanation: A direct question ends with a question mark.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly punctuates a quotation that itself contains a question?
options: "Where are you going?" she asked.
"Where are you going," she asked?
"Where are you going." she asked?
"Where are you going"? she asked.
questions.explanation: The question mark belongs inside the quotation because the quoted words form the question.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly punctuates a quotation that expresses strong emotion?
options: "Be careful!" the driver shouted.
"Be careful," the driver shouted!
"Be careful." the driver shouted!
"Be careful"! the driver shouted.
questions.explanation: The exclamation mark belongs inside the quotation because the quoted words are an exclamation.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses a period with an abbreviation?
options: Dr Smith examined the patient.
Dr. Smith examined the patient.
Dr; Smith examined the patient.
Dr: Smith examined the patient.
questions.explanation: Dr. is a common abbreviation for Doctor and is written with a period in this style.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses an apostrophe for a singular possessive?
options: The teachers desk was covered with books.
The teachers' desk was covered with books.
The teacher's desk was covered with books.
The teacher desk's was covered with books.
questions.explanation: A singular noun normally forms possession with 's.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses an apostrophe for an irregular plural possessive?
options: The childrens' playground was renovated.
The children's playground was renovated.
The childrens playground was renovated.
The children's' playground was renovated.
questions.explanation: Children is an irregular plural, so possession takes 's.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses its?
options: The machine lost it's power suddenly.
The machine lost its power suddenly.
The machine lost its' power suddenly.
The machine lost it's' power suddenly.
questions.explanation: Its is the possessive form; it's means it is or it has.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses it's?
options: The building has lost it's roof.
The building has lost its roof.
It's been damaged by the storm.
The building's roof is it's strongest feature.
questions.explanation: It's is correct because it means it has in 'It's been damaged.'

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses a colon before an explanation?
options: There was one reason for his absence: he was ill.
There was one reason for his absence, he was ill.
There was one reason for his absence; he was ill:
There was one reason: for his absence he was ill.
questions.explanation: The colon introduces the explanation of the stated reason.

questions.questionText: Which sentence uses a colon incorrectly?
options: She had one objective: to finish the project.
The box contained three items: a pen, a ruler, and a notebook.
My favorite subjects are: English and Biology.
He remembered one important rule: never give up.
questions.explanation: A colon should not normally separate a verb directly from its complement.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses a semicolon between independent clauses?
options: The lecture ended; the students left quietly.
The lecture ended; because the students left quietly.
The lecture; ended the students left quietly.
The lecture ended,; the students left quietly.
questions.explanation: Both sides are independent clauses, so a semicolon is appropriate.

questions.questionText: Which sentence incorrectly uses a semicolon?
options: The weather was cold; we continued hiking.
She wanted to study; her brother wanted to sleep.
Because it was late; we returned home.
The exam was difficult; everyone remained focused.
questions.explanation: Because it was late is a dependent clause and cannot normally stand independently after a semicolon.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly fixes the comma splice?
options: The road was blocked, we took another route.
The road was blocked; we took another route.
The road was blocked, because we took another route.
The road was blocked: and we took another route.
questions.explanation: A semicolon correctly joins the two closely related independent clauses.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses an ellipsis to show hesitation?
options: I... I don't know what to say.
I; I don't know what to say.
I: I don't know what to say.
I, I don't know what to say.
questions.explanation: An ellipsis can indicate hesitation or an unfinished thought.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses an ellipsis to indicate a trailing thought?
options: If only I had known...
If only I had known;
If only I had known:
If only I had known?
questions.explanation: An ellipsis can show that a thought trails off or remains unfinished.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses brackets inside a quotation?
options: "She [the minister] announced the decision yesterday."
"She (the minister) announced the decision yesterday."
"She—the minister—announced the decision yesterday."
"She, the minister, announced the decision yesterday."
questions.explanation: Brackets can add clarifying information inside quoted material.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses a dash rather than a hyphen?
options: The two countries signed a long-term agreement.
The answer was obvious—everyone already knew it.
She is a well-known author.
The meeting lasted twenty-one minutes.
questions.explanation: A dash creates a strong break or adds emphasis.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses a hyphen rather than a dash?
options: The decision was final—there was no appeal.
He is a highly respected—scientist.
She bought a part-time course.
The answer—according to him—was obvious.
questions.explanation: Part-time is a compound adjective joined with a hyphen.

questions.questionText: Which sentence is correctly punctuated?
options: The well known scientist presented a ten-year-old theory.
The well-known scientist presented a ten-year-old theory.
The well-known scientist presented a ten year-old theory.
The well known scientist presented a ten year old theory.
questions.explanation: Both compound adjectives before nouns require appropriate hyphenation.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses a comma after an introductory adverb?
options: However the results were disappointing.
However; the results were disappointing.
However, the results were disappointing.
However: the results were disappointing.
questions.explanation: A comma commonly follows an introductory word such as however.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly punctuates an introductory dependent clause?
options: If the weather improves we will leave early.
If the weather improves, we will leave early.
If, the weather improves we will leave early.
If the weather improves; we will leave early.
questions.explanation: The introductory dependent clause is separated from the main clause by a comma.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly punctuates an introductory participial phrase?
options: Having finished the assignment the student left.
Having finished the assignment, the student left.
Having finished, the assignment the student left.
Having finished the assignment; the student left.
questions.explanation: An introductory phrase is followed by a comma.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses commas around non-essential information?
options: Ethiopia which is in East Africa has a long history.
Ethiopia, which is in East Africa, has a long history.
Ethiopia which is in East Africa, has a long history.
Ethiopia, which is in East Africa has a long history.
questions.explanation: The non-essential relative clause requires commas on both sides.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly punctuates an essential relative clause?
options: The students, who submitted the forms, were admitted.
The students who submitted the forms were admitted.
The students who submitted the forms, were admitted.
The students, who submitted the forms were admitted.
questions.explanation: When the relative clause identifies which students are meant, commas are not used.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses commas with a person's name in direct address?
options: Can you help me Dawit?
Can you help me, Dawit?
Can you, help me Dawit?
Can you help, me Dawit?
questions.explanation: The name is a direct address and is separated by a comma.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly punctuates a series?
options: The course covers grammar, vocabulary, reading and writing.
The course covers grammar vocabulary, reading, and writing.
The course covers grammar, vocabulary, reading, and writing.
The course covers, grammar, vocabulary, reading, and writing.
questions.explanation: Commas separate the items in the series.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses the Oxford comma?
options: She bought bread, cheese and fruit.
She bought bread, cheese, and fruit.
She bought bread cheese, and fruit.
She bought bread, cheese; and fruit.
questions.explanation: The Oxford comma appears before and in a three-item list.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses punctuation with two independent clauses joined by but?
options: He wanted to leave but his friend stayed.
He wanted to leave, but his friend stayed.
He wanted to leave; but his friend stayed.
He wanted to leave: but his friend stayed.
questions.explanation: A comma precedes but when it joins two independent clauses.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses punctuation with yet?
options: The evidence was weak yet the court accepted it.
The evidence was weak, yet the court accepted it.
The evidence was weak; yet the court accepted it.
The evidence was weak: yet the court accepted it.
questions.explanation: Yet is a coordinating conjunction joining two independent clauses.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses punctuation with so?
options: The road was dangerous, so we turned back.
The road was dangerous; so we turned back.
The road was dangerous: so we turned back.
The road was dangerous so, we turned back.
questions.explanation: A comma precedes so when it joins two independent clauses.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses punctuation with for as a coordinating conjunction?
options: She stayed home, for she was feeling ill.
She stayed home; for she was feeling ill.
She stayed home: for she was feeling ill.
She stayed home for, she was feeling ill.
questions.explanation: For is a coordinating conjunction and takes a comma when joining independent clauses.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses punctuation with nor?
options: He did not apologize, nor did he explain his actions.
He did not apologize nor, did he explain his actions.
He did not apologize; nor did he explain his actions.
He did not apologize: nor did he explain his actions.
questions.explanation: A comma can precede nor when it joins two independent clauses.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses a colon after a complete clause?
options: There is one thing I need: your signature.
There is one thing: I need your signature.
There is: one thing I need your signature.
There is one thing I need, your signature:
questions.explanation: The complete clause introduces the specific information after the colon.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses a colon to introduce a list?
options: You need three items: a passport, a pen, and a notebook.
You need: a passport, a pen, and a notebook.
You need three items, a passport: a pen, and a notebook.
You need three items; a passport, a pen, and a notebook.
questions.explanation: The complete clause before the colon introduces the list.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses punctuation around a parenthetical expression?
options: The meeting, as expected (started late).
The meeting (as expected) started late.
The meeting as expected (started late).
The meeting (as expected, started late).
questions.explanation: The parenthetical information is enclosed in parentheses.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses an apostrophe in a contraction?
options: Theyre planning to leave early.
They're planning to leave early.
Theyre' planning to leave early.
They'r planning to leave early.
questions.explanation: They're is the contraction of they are.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses an apostrophe in a contraction?
options: Ive finished the assignment.
I've finished the assignment.
I' ve finished the assignment.
Ive' finished the assignment.
questions.explanation: I've is the contraction of I have.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses an apostrophe in a plural possessive?
options: The teachers room is upstairs.
The teacher's room is upstairs.
The teachers' room is upstairs.
The teachers's room is upstairs.
questions.explanation: Teachers is a regular plural, so possession takes an apostrophe after s.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses punctuation with a direct quotation introduced by a reporting clause?
options: He said "The results are final."
He said, "The results are final."
He said; "The results are final."
He said: "The results are final."
questions.explanation: A comma is the common punctuation separating the reporting clause from direct speech.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly punctuates speech followed by a reporting clause?
options: "I will return tomorrow," she said.
"I will return tomorrow." she said.
"I will return tomorrow"; she said.
"I will return tomorrow," She said.
questions.explanation: A comma normally precedes the closing quotation mark when the reporting clause follows.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly punctuates a quoted question followed by a reporting clause?
options: "Did you finish the work?" she asked.
"Did you finish the work," she asked?
"Did you finish the work." she asked.
"Did you finish the work"? she asked.
questions.explanation: The question mark belongs inside the quotation because the quoted words form the direct question.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly punctuates an interrupted quotation?
options: "I wanted to go," she said, "but I was too tired."
"I wanted to go" she said "but I was too tired."
"I wanted to go," she said; "but I was too tired."
"I wanted to go." she said, "but I was too tired."
questions.explanation: Commas can separate an inserted reporting clause within a continuous quotation.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses punctuation after an introductory name or title?
options: Dr. Ahmed, please examine the document.
Dr Ahmed please, examine the document.
Dr. Ahmed please examine, the document.
Dr Ahmed; please examine the document.
questions.explanation: The name/title functions as direct address and is followed by a comma.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses a dash to add an afterthought?
options: She finally answered the question—but only after several minutes.
She finally answered the question, but—only after several minutes.
She finally answered the question;—only after several minutes.
She finally answered the question: but only after several minutes.
questions.explanation: The dash emphasizes the additional information.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly distinguishes a hyphen from a dash?
options: The researcher was well-known—for her careful methods.
The researcher was well—known for her careful methods.
The researcher was well known—for her careful methods.
The researcher was well;known for her careful methods.
questions.explanation: Well-known is a compound adjective, while the dash introduces additional emphasis.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses a period rather than a question mark?
options: I wonder where the students are?
I wonder where the students are.
I wonder where are the students.
I wonder where the students are!
questions.explanation: I wonder where the students are is an indirect question and normally ends with a period.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses punctuation with an indirect question?
options: She asked whether the report was ready?
She asked whether was the report ready.
She asked whether the report was ready.
She asked, whether the report was ready?
questions.explanation: An indirect question has statement word order and ends with a period.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses punctuation after a warning?
options: Watch out.
Watch out?
Watch out!
Watch out;
questions.explanation: A strong warning commonly takes an exclamation mark.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses a semicolon in a contrast between closely related ideas?
options: The first method is inexpensive; the second is more reliable.
The first method is inexpensive, the second is more reliable.
The first method; is inexpensive the second is more reliable.
The first method is inexpensive: the second is more reliable.
questions.explanation: A semicolon appropriately joins two closely related independent clauses.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses a semicolon in a complex list?
options: The delegates came from Addis Ababa, Ethiopia; Nairobi, Kenya; and Cairo, Egypt.
The delegates came from Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, Nairobi, Kenya, and Cairo, Egypt.
The delegates came from Addis Ababa; Ethiopia, Nairobi; Kenya, and Cairo; Egypt.
The delegates came from Addis Ababa, Ethiopia: Nairobi, Kenya: and Cairo, Egypt.
questions.explanation: Semicolons separate list items that already contain commas.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses a colon followed by an explanation?
options: He could not attend the meeting: he was abroad.
He could not attend the meeting, he was abroad.
He could not attend the meeting; because he was abroad.
He could not attend: the meeting he was abroad.
questions.explanation: A colon can introduce an explanation of the preceding complete clause.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses parentheses without disrupting the main sentence?
options: The results (which were unexpected) changed the research plan.
The results, which were unexpected) changed the research plan.
The results (which were unexpected, changed the research plan.
The results which were (unexpected changed) the research plan.
questions.explanation: The complete parenthetical expression is enclosed by matching parentheses.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses an ellipsis in dialogue?
options: "Well... I suppose you are right."
"Well; I suppose you are right."
"Well: I suppose you are right."
"Well, ... I suppose you are right."
questions.explanation: An ellipsis naturally indicates hesitation in dialogue.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses an apostrophe for a possessive plural?
options: The women's committee met yesterday.
The womens' committee met yesterday.
The womens committee met yesterday.
The women's' committee met yesterday.
questions.explanation: Women is an irregular plural, so the possessive is women's.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses punctuation to separate contrasting clauses?
options: The first proposal was rejected, but the second was accepted.
The first proposal was rejected but, the second was accepted.
The first proposal was rejected; but the second was accepted.
The first proposal was rejected: but the second was accepted.
questions.explanation: A comma before but joins the two independent clauses.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly punctuates an introductory adverbial phrase?
options: In spite of the difficulties the project continued.
In spite of the difficulties, the project continued.
In spite, of the difficulties the project continued.
In spite of the difficulties; the project continued.
questions.explanation: A comma separates the introductory phrase from the main clause.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses punctuation with a long introductory phrase?
options: After completing the final stage of the experiment the researchers published their findings.
After completing the final stage of the experiment, the researchers published their findings.
After completing the final stage, of the experiment the researchers published their findings.
After completing the final stage of the experiment; the researchers published their findings.
questions.explanation: The long introductory phrase is followed by a comma.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly punctuates a sentence with a non-essential phrase?
options: The manager, after reviewing the report, approved the proposal.
The manager after reviewing the report approved the proposal.
The manager, after reviewing the report approved the proposal.
The manager after reviewing the report, approved the proposal.
questions.explanation: The non-essential phrase is enclosed by commas.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses punctuation to separate an appositive?
options: Mr. Bekele the director of the company spoke first.
Mr. Bekele, the director of the company, spoke first.
Mr. Bekele; the director of the company spoke first.
Mr. Bekele: the director of the company spoke first.
questions.explanation: The non-essential appositive is enclosed by commas.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses punctuation with a restrictive identifier?
options: My friend, Dawit, won the competition.
My friend Dawit won the competition.
My friend; Dawit won the competition.
My friend: Dawit won the competition.
questions.explanation: When the name identifies which friend is meant, commas are unnecessary.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses an apostrophe in a contraction?
options: Its been raining all morning.
It's been raining all morning.
Its' been raining all morning.
It'is been raining all morning.
questions.explanation: It's means it has in this sentence.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses an apostrophe to show possession?
options: The dog wagged it's tail.
The dog wagged its tail.
The dog wagged its' tail.
The dog wagged it tail's.
questions.explanation: Its is the possessive form of it.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses punctuation after a reporting verb when introducing a direct command?
options: The officer shouted, "Stop immediately!"
The officer shouted; "Stop immediately!"
The officer shouted "Stop immediately!"
The officer shouted: "Stop immediately!"
questions.explanation: A comma commonly introduces direct speech after a reporting clause.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly punctuates a direct quotation containing a period?
options: She said, "The examination begins at nine."
She said, "The examination begins at nine".
She said; "The examination begins at nine."
She said "The examination begins at nine".
questions.explanation: The quoted complete statement ends with a period inside the quotation marks.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses punctuation with a quoted title of a short work?
options: We discussed "The Road Not Taken" in class.
We discussed The Road Not Taken. in class.
We discussed "The Road Not Taken." in class.
We discussed: "The Road Not Taken" in class.
questions.explanation: Quotation marks can identify titles of shorter works under relevant style conventions.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses a dash to mark an interruption?
options: I was about to explain—but the alarm interrupted me.
I was about to explain, but—the alarm interrupted me.
I was about to explain;—the alarm interrupted me.
I was about to explain: but the alarm interrupted me.
questions.explanation: A dash can mark a sudden break or interruption.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses punctuation to separate two independent clauses without a conjunction?
options: The evidence was incomplete, the judge postponed the decision.
The evidence was incomplete; the judge postponed the decision.
The evidence was incomplete, and the judge postponed the decision.
The evidence was incomplete: and the judge postponed the decision.
questions.explanation: A semicolon joins two closely related independent clauses without a conjunction.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses a period to separate independent clauses?
options: The evidence was incomplete. The judge postponed the decision.
The evidence was incomplete, The judge postponed the decision.
The evidence was incomplete; The judge postponed the decision.
The evidence was incomplete: The judge postponed the decision.
questions.explanation: A period correctly separates the two complete sentences.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses punctuation after a direct address at the end?
options: Please close the door John.
Please close the door, John.
Please close the door; John.
Please close the door: John.
questions.explanation: A comma separates the person's name from the rest of the sentence.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses a comma before a coordinating conjunction?
options: The students were tired, but they continued studying.
The students were tired but, they continued studying.
The students were tired; but they continued studying.
The students were tired: but they continued studying.
questions.explanation: But joins two independent clauses and is preceded by a comma.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses punctuation in a sentence with an introductory clause and a quotation?
options: When the teacher arrived she said, "Begin the test."
When the teacher arrived, she said, "Begin the test."
When the teacher arrived; she said, "Begin the test."
When the teacher arrived she said "Begin the test."
questions.explanation: The introductory dependent clause takes a comma, and the reporting clause takes a comma before direct speech.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses punctuation with a parenthetical expression and a quotation?
options: The teacher (as usual) said, "Begin the test."
The teacher, (as usual), said "Begin the test."
The teacher (as usual), said; "Begin the test."
The teacher as usual, said, "Begin the test."
questions.explanation: Parentheses contain the extra information, while a comma introduces the quotation.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses a colon after a complete sentence to introduce a result?
options: He made one mistake: he ignored the warning.
He made one mistake, he ignored the warning.
He made one mistake; because he ignored the warning.
He made one mistake: because he ignored the warning.
questions.explanation: The colon introduces an explanation of the mistake.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses a dash to introduce a conclusion?
options: There was only one possible outcome—the plan failed.
There was only one possible outcome, the plan failed.
There was only one possible outcome; the plan failed—.
There was only one possible outcome:—the plan failed.
questions.explanation: A dash can introduce an emphasized conclusion or explanation.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses a hyphen in a compound adjective?
options: It was a highly successful research-based project.
It was a highly successful research based project.
It was a highly-successful research-based project.
It was a highly successful research—based project.
questions.explanation: Research-based is a compound adjective; highly successful does not normally require a hyphen.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses a hyphen with a compound number?
options: She is twenty one years old.
She is twenty-one years old.
She is twenty-one-years old.
She is twenty one-years-old.
questions.explanation: Compound numbers from twenty-one through ninety-nine are hyphenated.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses a hyphen when the age functions as a compound adjective?
options: She is a twenty-one-year-old student.
She is a twenty one year old student.
She is a twenty-one-years-old student.
She is a twenty-one-year old student.
questions.explanation: The complete compound adjective before the noun is hyphenated.
